title: US Ends 'Duration of Status' for Student Visas, Caps Stays at Four Years
excerpt: A new DHS rule effective September 15 eliminates open-ended stays for F-1 and J-1 visa holders, requiring USCIS extensions for programs longer than four years. India, the top source of international students, says it is monitoring the situation.
body:
• DHS published a final rule on July 17, 2026, eliminating the decades-old "duration of status" policy for F-1, J-1, and I visa holders, effective September 15, 2026.
  • International students and exchange visitors will be capped at four-year stays and must apply to USCIS for extensions, with background checks, biometric screening, and fees exceeding $2,400.
  • The post-graduation grace period for F-1 students is cut from 60 to 30 days, and universities lose the authority to approve transfers and program changes.
  • India — the largest source of international students in the US with roughly 330,000 enrolled — says it is in contact with Washington to "minimise difficulties" for its citizens.

The US Department of Homeland Security has finalized a sweeping regulation that ends nearly five decades of flexible visa arrangements for international students, exchange visitors, and foreign journalists. The rule, published in the Federal Register on July 17 and set to take effect on September 15, 2026, replaces the open-ended "duration of status" system with fixed admission periods capped at four years.

The change affects three visa categories: F visas for international students, J visas for cultural and educational exchange visitors, and I visas for foreign journalists. Roughly 1.2 million F-1 students, 500,000 J-1 exchange visitors, and 37,000 foreign media professionals currently in the United States will be impacted, according to the Migration Policy Institute and the US State Department.

What Changes on September 15

Under the previous system, established by the Immigration and Naturalization Service in 1978, international students could remain in the US for as long as their academic program required. Universities held the authority to approve transfers, program extensions, and changes of study through the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) database.

The new framework strips that authority from universities and hands it to US Citizenship and Immigration Services. Students who need more than four years — a common scenario given that more than 50% of bachelor's degree recipients take longer than four years to graduate, and the median doctoral student spends nearly six years on a dissertation, according to Brookings — must now file a formal application with USCIS. Extension requests will be subject to background checks, biometric screening, and fraud reviews, with application fees exceeding $400 and optional premium processing costing over $2,000.

The rule also cuts the post-graduation grace period for F-1 students from 60 days to 30 days. Current visa holders already in the US will automatically transition to the new framework, with their authorized stay capped at four years from the rule's effective date.

"For nearly half a century, the outdated 'duration of status' system has compromised national security and created an environment ripe for immigration fraud."

— Markwayne Mullin, DHS Secretary

The Economic Stakes

Education advocacy groups and economists have pushed back sharply. A study commissioned by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine estimated the regulation could cost the US economy $72 billion to $145 billion annually over the next decade — more than 22 times the $3.3 billion DHS identified as the rule's ten-year cost.

NAFSA, the Association of International Educators, projects a more immediate hit: $7 billion in lost revenue and more than 60,000 jobs if the policy discourages international enrollment. International students contributed $42.9 billion to the US economy and supported 355,736 jobs in the 2024-25 academic year, according to NAFSA data.

The rule arrives as US universities already face a 20% drop in international student applications. A survey by the Institute for Progress and NAFSA found that 49% of current international graduate students and postdoctoral researchers would not have enrolled if this regulation had been in place.

"At a time when global competition for talent is intensifying, this policy sends exactly the wrong message. It tells the world's brightest students and scholars that the United States is becoming less welcoming, less predictable, and less committed."

— Fanta Aw, CEO, NAFSA

Impact on Indian Students

India currently sends the largest number of international students to the United States, with approximately 330,000 enrolled in US academic institutions during the 2023-24 academic year, according to India's Ministry of External Affairs. The new rule threatens to disrupt pathways that have made the US the top destination for Indian students pursuing STEM degrees, medical training, and doctoral research.

New Delhi has signaled concern. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal confirmed that India is in contact with Washington over the changes. "As and when there are issues of difficulties which are brought to our attention in regard to genuine travellers and students, we take up those issues with the US side so as to minimise the difficulties that our people face," Jaiswal said at a media briefing.

The regulation could be especially disruptive for Indian medical graduates. International physicians account for nearly 25% of the US physician workforce, and many critical residency and fellowship programs — including general surgery, geriatrics, and cardiology — cannot be completed within four years. The International Medical Graduate Taskforce stated it would be "impossible" for physicians to finish many training programs under the new cap.

What Happens Next

The rule is subject to congressional scrutiny under the Congressional Review Act, and a bipartisan group of four congressional representatives has already urged DHS to delay implementation. The regulation drew over 20,000 public comments during the rulemaking process. DHS estimates it will generate more than 400,000 additional USCIS applications annually — a 163% increase for this application type — at a time when the agency's backlog already exceeds 11.3 million cases.

Legal challenges are also possible. A similar 2018 proposal was blocked by a preliminary court injunction. The first Trump administration appealed but later withdrew the appeal. This time, DHS used the formal notice-and-comment rulemaking process to try to insulate the rule from procedural challenges, though critics argue the agency failed to adequately address the concerns raised in public comments.

For Indian students weighing fall 2026 enrollment decisions or planning graduate programs, the September 15 effective date leaves little time to adjust. The rule could accelerate a shift already underway, with international students increasingly choosing Australia, Canada, and the UK over the United States.
nri_angle: India sends the most international students to the US, with roughly 330,000 enrolled, and the new four-year cap and extension requirements could disrupt academic and career pathways for Indian students pursuing STEM, medical, and doctoral programs.
